passage:
Pankaj, fourteen, sat in the school counsellor's room, arms wrapped around his middle.
"Your stomach again?" Gurleen Ma'am asked.
"It's nothing. Papa says I'm doing drama to skip school." His voice cracked. "So I stopped telling him."
She didn't laugh or doubt him. "Pain is real even when tests don't show a cause. How long has it been happening?"
"Since the new term. Mostly mornings."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm going to call your parents today and suggest a proper check with a doctor, so we know your body is okay. And then, if you want, we can talk about what mornings feel like."
Pankaj looked up. "You believe me?"
"I do."
That evening his mother took him to the clinic. And on Thursday, Pankaj came back to Gurleen Ma'am's room and talked about how scared he'd been of the new class.

qa.q: When does Pankaj's stomach pain mostly happen?
qa.a: Mostly in the mornings, since the new term.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Papa called it drama?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unheard, so he stopped telling Papa about the pain.

qa.q: How did Gurleen Ma'am open the way for Pankaj to talk?
qa.a: She believed him, called his parents that day to arrange a doctor's check, and offered to talk about his mornings when he was ready.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother have felt after Gurleen Ma'am's call?
qa.a: She was probably concerned enough to act, since she took him to the clinic that very evening.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose pain was dismissed as attention-seeking hiding his distress, and how taking the symptoms seriously opens the way to talking about stress.

passage:
Dear Papa,

Mumma says I should write this down because I get tongue-tied when I try to say it, so here it is.
Last Sunday, when I said my head hurt again, you said, "Enough drama, Sunaina, you just don't want to study." I know you were tired. But it really hurt, Papa. Not just my head. That you didn't believe me.
Since then I've been hiding it. I take my books to the terrace so you won't see me rubbing my forehead. Some days I feel dizzy and I still don't say anything.
I'm not trying to get out of studying. I think maybe I'm stressed about the board exams, and my body is showing it. Can we please go to the doctor to check? And after that, can we talk?

Love,
Sunaina

P.S. Mumma says, "Sahil, read it twice."

qa.q: Where does Sunaina take the books to hide the pain?
qa.a: Sunaina takes the books to the terrace.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Papa called it drama?
qa.a: Sunaina felt hurt and disbelieved, which hurt even more than the headache.

qa.q: What does Sunaina ask for, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: A doctor's check and then a talk, because taking the pain seriously could also open up the stress about the board exams.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Papa might feel sorry and surprised to learn that those words made Sunaina hide the pain and dizziness.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose headaches were dismissed as drama feeling unheard and hiding distress, and asking for the symptoms to be checked and the stress talked about.

passage: Divyansh, you think I don't understand when you say your stomach hurts? Sit. Let your Ma, Shalini, tell you about when I was fifteen. Before every exam my stomach twisted so badly I couldn't eat. I told my father. He said, 'Stop this drama. You just want to skip school.' So I stopped telling anyone. I'd sit in the school toilet during lunch, bent over, and pretend I was fine. It got worse. My aunt finally noticed me sitting alone and took me to the doctor, who checked me carefully and said my stomach was healthy but my mind was carrying a lot. Then she asked me, 'What's frightening you?' And I cried and told her everything about the marks and my father. That's why, when you say it hurts, I will always listen.

qa.q: Where did young Shalini sit during lunch?
qa.a: In the school toilet.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel when her father called it drama?
qa.a: She felt unheard and hurt, and stopped telling anyone about her pain.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shalini's story?
qa.a: Her aunt took her pain seriously, took her to the doctor, and then asked what was frightening her.

qa.q: How might Shalini's aunt have felt seeing her sitting alone?
qa.a: She was probably concerned and caring enough to take action.

grounding: Shows, through a mother's memory, a teenager whose pain was dismissed as drama, who hid her distress until an aunt took it seriously and opened talk about stress.

passage: Harsha's maths exam was tomorrow, and her mother was away at a conference. Harsha, fifteen, had had headaches for two weeks. When she mentioned it at dinner, her father, Hemant, rolled his eyes. 'Every time there's a test, you get a headache. It's drama so you can skip tuition.' Harsha went to her room and didn't mention it again. That night her head pounded so badly she was sick. Hemant heard her in the bathroom and found her pale and shaking. He sat on the edge of the bath, suddenly ashamed. 'I'm sorry. I didn't take you seriously.' He rang the family doctor, who saw them that evening and found no illness but asked how she was feeling about school. On the drive home Harsha told him about the pressure. He listened, all the way.

qa.q: Where was Harsha's mother?
qa.a: Away at a conference.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when her father called it drama?
qa.a: She felt unheard and hurt, so she stopped telling him about her headaches.

qa.q: What opened the way to talking about stress?
qa.a: Hemant apologised, took her symptoms seriously and to the doctor, and then listened on the drive home.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel finding Harsha sick in the bathroom?
qa.a: He felt suddenly ashamed and worried for having dismissed her pain.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose headaches are dismissed as drama and who hides her distress, until a parent takes them seriously and a medical check opens talk about stress.

passage: Ishita, fourteen, had been getting stomach aches and a tight chest for weeks, ever since her friend group fell apart. Her mother Sarita sighed every time she mentioned it. 'Ishita, you're just trying to get out of school. Stop the attention-seeking.' So Ishita stopped mentioning it. She sat alone at lunch, clutching her stomach, and cried quietly in bed at night. One evening, Sarita heard her through the door. She stood there a long time. Then she went in and sat on the bed. 'I'm sorry. I thought you were exaggerating.' Ishita turned away. 'You never believe me.' 'I believe you now. Tomorrow we're going to the doctor, and then you can tell me what's really going on.' The doctor found nothing serious. On the way back, Ishita told her about the friends.

qa.q: When did Ishita's stomach aches start?
qa.a: Ever since her friend group fell apart.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when her mother called it attention-seeking?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unheard, and stopped talking about her pain.

qa.q: What changed when Sarita took Ishita seriously?
qa.a: The doctor's visit and Sarita's apology made space for Ishita to talk about the real stress with her friends.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling as she stood outside the door?
qa.a: She was probably shaken and guilty, realising how upset her daughter was.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose symptoms are dismissed as attention-seeking and who hides her pain, until her mother takes it seriously and a doctor's check opens talk about stress.

passage:
"Mummy, my stomach hurts again."
"Again? Every day before school, Disha. It's drama." Indu kept rolling the rotis.
"It's not drama. It really hurts."
"Last week it was your head. Next it'll be your toe."
Disha went to her room and shut the door softly. That evening she didn't come for dinner.
Indu knocked. "Disha? Aren't you eating?"
"Why? You'll just say I'm faking."
Silence. Then Indu came in and sat on the bed. "I said drama because I was scared it was something else, and I was tired. That wasn't fair." She paused. "Tomorrow we'll see Dr Kamath. Both things: we check your stomach, and you tell me what's happening at school."
Disha's eyes filled. "The maths sir shouts at me every day."
Indu took her hand. "Then tell me now. I'm listening."

qa.q: Which doctor does Indu say they will see?
qa.a: Dr Kamath.

qa.q: Why did Disha skip dinner?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unheard after being called dramatic, and expected to be told she was faking.

qa.q: What did Indu change that opened the way to talking?
qa.a: She admitted that dismissing the pain wasn't fair, promised a medical check, and asked about school, which let Disha share the real worry.

qa.q: Why might Indu have reacted with "It's drama" at first?
qa.a: She admits she was scared it was something else and was tired, so brushing it off felt easier than worrying.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose pain is dismissed as drama feeling unheard, and a parent who takes it seriously, plans a medical check and opens the way to talk about stress.
